+ Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 74.8
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The sleek, matte-black smartwatch had no brand name, no charger, and no instruction manual. I’d found it half-buried in a box of old calculators at a garage sale on Elm Street. The creepy old man running the sale just smiled a toothless grin and said, "Take it, kid. Time is on your side." I should have known garage sales on Elm Street were bad news. My name is Leo Granger, and until Tuesday, my biggest problem was surviving seventh grade. Now, my biggest problem is surviving the space-time continuum. The watch’s secret revealed itself during third-period lunch. I had just tripped over my own untied shoelace, launching my cafeteria tray into the air. A perfectly square slice of pepperoni pizza slapped right onto the forehead of Todd "The Tank" Henderson. The cafeteria erupted in laughter. Todd’s face turned the color of a crushed tomato. Panicking, I squeezed my eyes shut and desperately twisted the watch’s only dial backward. *Click. Click. Click.* A weird, icy shiver zipped down my spine. My bones ached, like my skeleton was stretching. When I opened my eyes, I wasn't on the floor. I was back in line, holding my tray. Todd was two tables away, pizza-free. I checked the watch. 11:45 AM. Five minutes ago. I’d rewound time. I spent the rest of the week treating life like a video game. Failed a pop quiz in Mr. Harrison’s math class? *Click, click.* Rewind, memorize the answers, get an A. Said something totally awkward to Chloe, the girl I’d liked since fourth grade? *Click, click.* Rewind, say something cool instead. It was the ultimate cheat code. But I was so obsessed with fixing my mistakes, I didn't notice the glitch in the system. It started on Thursday morning. I was walking past the bike racks when I saw the stray cat. It was a scruffy, one-eared orange tabby that always hung around the dumpsters. Usually, it bolted when kids got near. But this time, it sat dead still, its unblinking yellow eyes locked onto me. It didn't look scared. It looked... disappointed. It let out a low, raspy yowl that sounded almost human, then slinked into the bushes. "Weird cat," I muttered. My voice sounded strange. Deeper. Like I was talking into a hollow barrel. When I got to my locker, my favorite denim jacket felt suffocatingly tight across my shoulders. My sneakers pinched my toes so badly I had to loosen the laces. "Hey, Leo," Chloe said, walking up beside me. She blinked, tilting her head. "Did you get a haircut? Or... wait. Did you get taller?" "Uh, maybe a growth spurt?" I squeaked. Actually, I didn't squeak. My voice rumbled like a bass drum. "And is that... fuzz on your upper lip?" she asked, her nose wrinkling. I touched my face. Rough bristles poked my fingertips. I swallowed hard. I was twelve. I wasn't supposed to have a mustache. In the hallway, Mr. Harrison walked past. Instead of yelling at me to get to class, he gave me a polite nod. "Morning, young man. Visiting the middle school today?" *Visiting?* I thought. *I’m in your second-period class!* I rushed to the boys' bathroom and stared into the mirror above the sinks. The face staring back wasn't Leo Granger, seventh-grader. The cheeks had lost their roundness. The jaw was sharp, covered in a patchy, dark shadow of facial hair. My shoulders were broad, bursting the seams of my shirt. Every time I wound the watch backward, time moved backward for the world. But it moved *forward* for me. I was stealing time. I promised myself I wouldn't use it again. Never. Then came Friday. The school was holding its annual pep rally. The bleachers were packed. Chloe was on the top row, laughing with her friends. Todd The Tank was showing off, tossing a heavy basketball up and trying to catch it behind his back. He missed. The ball bounced hard off the wooden bleachers, rocketing straight toward the top row. It hit Chloe square in the chest. She tumbled backward, screaming, over the edge of the high bleachers. A sickening *CRACK* echoed through the gym. I didn't think. I didn't care about my tight shoes or my deep voice. I grabbed the dial on the black watch and twisted it hard. Not just a few clicks. I spun it. *Click-click-click-click-click-click!* The icy shiver hit me like a freight train. My joints popped. My muscles tore and rebuilt themselves in a fraction of a second. My spine stretched so violently I let out a guttural scream. The gym dissolved into a blur of swirling gray mist. When the mist cleared, I wasn't in the gym. I was standing outside in the freezing rain. I gasped for air. My lungs felt heavy. I looked down at my hands. They were huge, calloused, with thick veins popping through the skin. My clothes were shredded rags, completely outgrown. I looked up. Blackwood Middle School was gone. In its place stood a charred, blackened foundation overgrown with dead, twisting vines. A rusty chain-link fence surrounded the ruins. A faded sign hung crookedly on the gate: *CONDEMNED - 2015*. 2015? That was years ago. "Chloe?" I croaked. My voice was the gruff, gravelly sound of a thirty-year-old man. I spun around, looking at the street. The houses were boarded up. The sky was a sickly, bruised purple. By rewinding so far, so fast, I hadn't just changed the past. I had fractured the timeline. I had erased my school. I had erased my life. *Meow.* I froze. Sitting on the cracked pavement, completely untouched by the rain, was the one-eared orange tabby. Its yellow eyes burned into mine. It knew. It remembered the real world. "How do I fix this?" I begged the cat, my adult voice cracking with panic. The cat just stared at my wrist. I looked down at the matte-black watch. It was ticking backward now, all on its own. If I rewound it again—if I went back far enough to stop myself from ever buying the watch at that garage sale—I could fix the timeline. I could save Chloe. I could bring the town back. But I looked at my massive, aged hands. Every minute I rewound aged me. Going back days had turned me into a man. Going back weeks had destroyed the town. If I went back *months*... my body wouldn't survive it. I would age into dust before I ever reached Elm Street. The cat let out another raspy, hollow yowl. I took a deep breath, feeling the ache of old bones in my chest. I pinched the dial. And I started to twist.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of the prompt. It hits every required beat: the smartwatch with rewind power, the gradual unnoticed aging, the social shifts in how people treat Leo, the accidental catastrophic timeline shift, and the ambiguous "one more rewind" ending. The length lands right around the 1000-word seed. The Goosebumps register is well captured—first-person, punchy short paragraphs, wry asides ("I should have known garage sales on Elm Street were bad news"), and a slightly ominous, kid-friendly horror tone. Strengths: The escalation structure is clean and well-paced (pizza incident → casual abuse of power → physical signs → Chloe/Todd/Harrison reactions → gym disaster → ruined timeline). The aging is shown through concrete, age-appropriate details: tight jacket, pinching shoes, deepening voice, mustache fuzz, Mr. Harrison's "visiting the middle school today?"—which is a genuinely effective beat. The prose is economical and vivid without purple excess. The one-eared cat as a recurring uncanny witness is a nice genre touch, though its function as a knowing guide edges toward convenient. Weaknesses: The mechanics of the timeline fracture are fuzzy—rewinding time to save Chloe somehow erases the school and condemns it in 2015, and the causal link is hand-waved ("I had fractured the timeline"). The cat staring meaningfully at the watch is a bit of a plot crutch. The ending twist (the watch ticking backward on its own) is atmospheric but slightly convenient. Chloe and Todd are thin, functional characters; Leo himself is a serviceful genre everykid rather than nuanced. Some phrasing is stock ("hit me like a freight train," "color of a crushed tomato"). Dialogue is minimal and serviceable, not memorable. The final line is a solid cliffhanger, appropriately ominous for the genre, and the ambiguity ("maybe?") honors the prompt. Overall this is competent, engaging middle-grade horror that fulfills the brief with only minor hand-waving in its logic. + Noir romance: Carnival of Dangerous Intentions — Score: 71.6
Prompt:
Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The sodium lights were a relatively new addition to the boardwalk, bleeding a harsh, jaundiced yellow into the violet dusk. They flickered inconsistently, buzzing like trapped hornets and casting strange, elongated patterns across the faces of the passing crowds. The air smelled of roasted peanuts, brine, and the sharp, metallic tang of ozone. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery. *His locks.* The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else—dangerously compelling—quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger—the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. *Why am I here?* Evelyn asked herself, her fingers gripping her beaded clutch until her knuckles ached beneath her silk gloves. *It is madness. I am an engaged woman. I belong in Manhattan, in a parlor, not slumming in the shadows of the Cyclone.* Yet, the thrill of her own disobedience sent a flush of heat up her neck. He was already there. He leaned against the chipped wooden counter of the gallery, a silhouette carved out of the carnival's chaotic glare. He wore no jacket, only a crisp white shirt with the sleeves rolled up to the elbows, revealing forearms corded with lean muscle. As the sodium light spasmed, it illuminated his face. His eyes caught hers through the crowd. They were fathomless, entirely devoid of the polite deference she was accustomed to from men. "You're late," he said as she stepped up beside him. His voice was a low timbre that seemed to vibrate beneath her ribs. "I wasn't aware we had set a specific hour," Evelyn replied, lifting her chin. "Only evening." "Dusk is a precise moment. It’s the second the sun surrenders to the dark." He turned his body toward her, invading her personal space by a fraction of an inch. "I thought perhaps your courage had failed you." "I am not a coward." "No?" A slow, devastating smile touched his lips. "Then why are you trembling?" "It is the ocean breeze. Nothing more." *Liar,* a voice whispered in her mind. *You are trembling because he is looking at you as if you are the prize on the top shelf.* The proximity of him was intoxicating. She could smell bay rum, clean sweat, and the faint, acrid scent of gunpowder from the gallery. He turned to the carnival barker, tossing a silver dime onto the counter. "Two rifles." "I don't shoot," Evelyn said quickly. "You will tonight." He picked up the heavy Winchester pump-action gallery gun and held it out to her. The metal was worn smooth from thousands of hands. "Take it." "I told you, I don't—" "Take it," he repeated, his voice dropping a full octave, laced with a velvet authority that made her breath hitch. Evelyn reached out, her gloved hands accepting the wood and steel. It was heavier than she expected. "Good," he murmured. He picked up the second rifle and rested the butt against his hip. "Now, look at the ducks. The painted ones moving in the back row. They’re the hardest to hit. The trick is not to aim where they are, but where they are going to be." "This is ridiculous. I am wearing a silk dress." "And you look exquisite in it. But the dress doesn't shoot the gun." He took a step closer, stepping behind her. The heat radiating from his chest ghosted against her back. "Raise the stock to your shoulder." She hesitated. *I should put this down. I should turn around, walk to the train, and never look back.* But the dark gravity of him held her pinned. Slowly, she lifted the rifle. "Tighter," he instructed. Suddenly, his hands were on her. One hand covered hers on the forestock, his long fingers wrapping over her silk glove. His other hand settled firmly on her waist, adjusting her stance. The touch was entirely improper, shocking in its possessive familiarity. "Spread your feet," he whispered, his lips mere inches from her ear. "You need a foundation, or the recoil will knock you off balance. Let me guide you." "I... I can't see the sights," she breathed, her voice betraying a damning tremor. The flickering lights above cast sharp, erratic shadows over the moving tin ducks, making them blur. "Don't look at the lights. Look through the shadows." His thumb stroked the inside of her wrist, a deliberate, agonizingly slow friction against the edge of her glove. "Squeeze the trigger. Don't pull it. Squeeze it like you're holding a secret you can't bear to let go of." *He knows,* she thought wildly. *He knows exactly what he is doing to me.* The moral ambiguity of the moment was a heavy, suffocating blanket. She was a woman of standing, allowing a nameless vagabond to handle her in public, to command her. And heaven help her, she wanted him to press closer. "Now," he commanded softly. Evelyn squeezed the trigger. The rifle cracked violently, jumping against her shoulder. The smell of sulfur bloomed in the damp air. At the back of the gallery, a small tin duck flipped backward with a sharp *ping*. "There," he murmured, his breath warm against her cheek. He didn't move away. His hand remained anchored on her waist, his grip tightening just a fraction, a subtle assertion of control. "You have a good eye. And a steady hand. When you allow yourself to." "It was luck," she said, lowering the barrel, though she made no move to step out of his embrace. "I don't believe in luck." He finally stepped back, though the absence of his heat felt like a sudden plunge into ice water. He set his own rifle down without firing a single shot. "I believe in intent. Why did you come back tonight?" "I wanted to see the carnival." "Another lie." He reached out, his bare fingers brushing a stray curl of hair behind her ear. The contact made her gasp softly. "You came because you wanted to know how far you would go before you stopped yourself." "And what if I don't want to stop?" she challenged, surprising herself with the reckless words. The sodium lights buzzed loudly, plunging them into a half-second of total darkness before flaring back to life. In that brief flash of light, his dark eyes gleamed with a predatory, ruinous hunger. "Then," he said quietly, "we are going to be a very dangerous problem for each other."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This scene delivers a competent, atmospheric rendition of the prompt: a 1937 Coney Island encounter charged with romantic danger. The writer successfully integrates the seed text and maintains the requested balance of dialogue (~50%), internal monologue (~20%), and exposition (~30%). The shooting gallery is a well-chosen setting—the rifle as an instrument of intimacy and control is an effective, if slightly on-the-nose, metaphor for the power dynamic. Strengths: The period details are mostly convincing (sodium lights, bay rum, beaded clutch, silk gloves, dime for the gallery). The dialogue carries the scene's tension well; lines like "Dusk is a precise moment. It's the second the sun surrenders to the dark" and "Squeeze it like you're holding a secret you can't bear to let go of" have a seductive, menacing cadence appropriate to the requested tone. The ending line—"we are going to be a very dangerous problem for each other"—lands the moral ambiguity the prompt asked for without tipping into melodrama. Weaknesses: The piece leans on genre clichés. The stranger is a stock dark-romance figure: obsidian curls, "fathomless" eyes, "predatory, ruinous hunger," rolled sleeves and corded forearms. Evelyn's characterization is thin—engaged woman, thrill-seeking, trembling—without much interior specificity beyond her arousal and guilt. Some phrasing is overwrought ("the dark gravity of him held her pinned," "the moral ambiguity of the moment was a heavy, suffocating blanket"—which is also a tell-don't-show lapse, naming the ambiguity rather than letting it breathe). The light-flicker blackout device is convenient and slightly theatrical. The physical escalation (hands on waist, wrist-stroking) follows a predictable Fifty-Shades-adjacent choreography rather than surprising the reader. Minor anachronism risk: "Winchester pump-action gallery gun" is plausible but the specificity feels like showing off. The prose occasionally strains for effect ("the sodium light spasmed"). Still, the scene is coherent, paced well, never meanders, and achieves its stated goal of establishing tension with a restrained classic sensibility. It is professional genre fiction—engaging but not inventive. + Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 78.8
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The trek back to the lodge was an exercise in suffocating silence. The Maine woods had always possessed a certain heavy stillness in late November, but today, the trees felt like a crowd of onlookers holding their collective breath. JT walked ten paces behind his father and Mike, his boots crunching through the frost-heaved crust of dead leaves and pine needles. Every snap sounded like a gunshot in the quiet, but neither of the men ahead of him so much as twitched. Usually, his dad would hiss at him to pick up his feet, to stop scaring off the game. Today, his father just walked with a slow, mechanical rhythm, his Woolrich jacket a dull red smudge against the encroaching gray twilight. JT kept his eyes on the back of his brother’s neck. *I didn’t see anything,* he told himself, the thought rhythmic and desperate, matching his stride. *Just the cold playing tricks. Just the glare off the frost.* But the image of his father reaching out to stroke the muzzle of that massive buck was burned into the back of his corneas, a surreal photograph he couldn't blink away. When they finally broke through the tree line and saw the lodge, JT felt no relief. The structure looked slumped, exhausted, its dark windows staring back at the woods like hollow eyes. Inside, the routine took over, though it felt like a pantomime. They stripped off their heavy blaze-orange coats. His father struck a match and got the ancient cast-iron woodstove going, while Mike began slicing the backstrap from the caribou they’d shot that morning—the one that had waited for the bullet. The meat hit the cast-iron skillet with a violent hiss. The smell of it filled the cramped kitchen, but it didn’t smell like venison. It lacked that rich, gamey iron tang. Instead, it smelled cloying, almost sickeningly sweet, like overripe fruit left to ferment in the sun. JT swallowed hard against a sudden wave of nausea, retreating to the battered corduroy sofa in the living room. "You quiet tonight, J-Bird," his father said. His voice was a low rasp that seemed to vibrate in the floorboards. JT looked up. His father was standing in the doorway, a spatula in one hand, staring at him. The man’s eyes looked glassy, catching the orange glow of the woodstove in a way that made his pupils look blown wide, entirely black. "Just tired," JT managed to say, forcing a weak smile. "Long drive." "Woods take it out of you," Mike chimed in from the kitchen. His voice sounded distant, hollowed out. "They ask for a lot. You just gotta know how to give it to 'em." JT’s stomach tightened. "Give what?" Mike didn’t answer. The sizzling in the pan grew louder, filling the silence. "You boys ever go up near the old Miller place today?" their father asked suddenly, turning back toward the stove. JT shivered. The Miller cabin was an old, rotting line shack about three miles up the northern ridge. It had been abandoned since the seventies, after old man Miller walked into the woods without his boots in the dead of January and never came back. Local legend—the kind whispered by the old-timers at the hardware store in town—said the cabin wasn't exactly empty. They said Miller had found something out there in the deep snow, something older than the pines, and brought it back. Hunters who strayed too close claimed they could hear a low, rhythmic humming coming from the collapsed chimney, a sound that made your teeth ache. "No," JT said quickly. "We stayed by the lower creek." "Good," his father murmured, though he didn't sound relieved. He sounded wistful. "They're gathering up that way. Best leave 'em to it." *Who is gathering?* JT wanted to ask. *The caribou? Or something else?* But the words piled up like dry sawdust in his throat. He realized, with a creeping sense of horror, that he was terrified of his own family. Dinner was an agonizing affair. His father and brother ate with a slow, methodical intensity, chewing the sweet, dark meat in perfect unison. JT pushed his portion around his chipped enamel plate, sneaking a bite only to hide it in his napkin when they weren't looking. The texture was wrong—too soft, almost melting on his tongue before he could spit it out. Whenever he glanced up, he found Mike staring at him, smiling a faint, knowing smile that didn't reach his eyes. "Eat up, JT," Mike whispered at one point, his fork scraping loudly against his plate. "You're gonna need your strength. The season's just starting." By the time JT retreated to his bunk in the back room, his nerves were frayed to the point of snapping. He crawled into his sleeping bag fully dressed, his hunting knife clutched tightly under his pillow. The wind picked up outside, whistling through the gaps in the cedar shingles, sounding uncomfortably like breath. He lay awake for hours, trapped in a liminal space between waking and a feverish sleep, haunted by visions of flat, dark caribou eyes and his father’s trembling, outstretched hand. He didn't know what time it was when the silence woke him. The wind had died completely. The lodge was dead quiet—too quiet. The familiar, rhythmic snoring of his brother from the bunk across the room was missing. JT sat up, his breath pluming in the freezing air of the bedroom. The woodstove had gone out. "Mike?" he whispered. Nothing. He slipped out of his sleeping bag, his boots thudding softly against the pine floorboards. He crept into the main room. It was empty. The front door of the lodge stood wide open, framing a rectangle of pale moonlight and snow. JT’s heart hammered against his ribs like a trapped bird. He moved to the doorway, his hand gripping the cold doorframe, and looked out into the clearing. There were dozens of them. The yard was filled with caribou, standing shoulder to shoulder in the moonlight. They were perfectly still, a sea of antlers casting jagged, intersecting shadows across the snow. They weren't grazing. They were all facing the lodge. Facing *him*. And out there, walking among them, were his father and Mike. They had stripped off their jackets and shirts, their bare skin pale and goose-pimpled in the freezing night. They were moving from animal to animal, their movements slow and reverent. JT watched, paralyzed by a terror so profound it felt like gravity, as his brother stopped before a massive buck. Mike reached out, just as their father had done earlier, but this time, he didn't stop at the muzzle. Mike leaned forward, pressing his forehead against the beast's skull. The caribou exhaled a long, pluming breath that seemed to envelop his brother. And then, in the dead silence of the winter night, JT heard it—a low, resonant humming, rising not from the animals, but from the throats of his father and brother. It was the sound from the Miller cabin. The buck slowly turned its head, its flat, dark eyes locking directly onto JT standing in the doorway. Then, all at once, every single caribou in the yard turned to look at him. And JT realized, with a mind-fracturing certainty, that they were waiting for him to join them.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The continuation effectively sustains the Stephen King register established in the prompt: grounded hunting-lodge realism, creeping dread, an isolated unreliable narrator, and dialogue that hints at complicity without explaining too much. The Miller cabin legend is a well-judged King-style piece of local folklore that pays off when the humming recurs at the climax. Dialogue is functional and appropriately eerie ("They ask for a lot. You just gotta know how to give it to 'em"), though a couple of lines lean slightly on genre stock phrasing ("You're gonna need your strength. The season's just starting"). The escalating sequence—wrong-smelling meat, synchronized eating, the silent night, the open door, the yard full of caribou—builds tension methodically toward a strong payoff image. JT's fear of his own family is convincingly rendered; his decision to hide food rather than confront anyone is psychologically believable for the established character. The ending, with the herd turning to face him, delivers on the seed requirement and lands the "waiting" motif seeded in the first chapter. Weaknesses: some familiar tropes (abandoned cabin with dark legend, blank-eyed animals, family members entranced) are well-executed but not novel; the climax borders on the expected for this genre. Occasional over-explanatory interiority ("a terror so profound it felt like gravity," "mind-fracturing certainty") tips into telling rather than showing, and a few phrases ("a surreal photograph he couldn't blink away") are slightly overwrought. The prose is generally controlled, with strong sensory details (cloying-sweet meat, breath-pluming cold, jagged antler shadows) and no purple excess. Word count is roughly appropriate. Character work is solid for horror's limited scope—JT is nuanced in his uncertainty and shame; father and Mike are deliberately flattened by the horror, which is acceptable. + Fantasy-humour: Hell is Other Demons — Score: 79.1
Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. 1000 words.
Model Output:
It was a Tuesday in Pandemonium, which meant the agonizing screams of the perpetually damned were running about a half-pitch flat. Lucifer Morningstar rubbed his temples, adjusting his immaculate bespoke suit, and stared at the towering stack of Torment Processing Sheets on his desk. *Crunch. Screeeeech. Snap.* Lucifer sighed, a sound like the dying breath of a suffocating star. "Barnaby. Drop it." Beneath the great Iron Throne of Hell, Barnaby paused. He was a purebred hellhound, roughly the size of a transit van, composed entirely of shadow, brimstone, and poor impulse control. The middle of his three heads looked up, a jagged chunk of wrought iron protruding from his jaws. The throne wobbled dangerously. "I said drop it," Lucifer repeated, not looking up from a requisition form for more mildly damp socks for the Department of Minor Inconveniences. Barnaby whined—a sound that caused three minor demons in the adjacent filing room to spontaneously combust—and spat the iron chunk onto the obsidian floor. He immediately began gnawing on the remaining stump of the throne’s front left leg. Lucifer didn't have the energy to scold him again. It had been three centuries since his last vacation, and fourteen months since Lilith had moved out. Again. Their relationship was cyclical. An aeon of passionate, world-ending romance, followed by a spectacular argument usually involving thrown galaxies or plagues, culminating in a period of stony silence. They were currently in the "off" phase. Or, at least, they were supposed to be. Lately, the silence had been punctuated by unannounced visits. She hadn't tried to assassinate him in weeks, which, in the demonic dating scene, was the equivalent of a late-night "u up?" text. The heavy mahogany doors of the throne room swung open, freezing the ambient lavafalls in their tracks. Lilith strode in. She wore a tailored charcoal trench coat over a dress woven from the despair of orphaned Victorian children—very vintage, very chic. She looked magnificent, terrifying, and profoundly annoyed. "Your layout in the Boiling Blood Lakes is entirely inefficient," she announced, bypassing the trembling imp at the reception desk. "They’re bottlenecking at the sulfur vents. It’s taking souls three hours just to get properly flayed. It’s embarrassing, Luce." Lucifer felt a familiar, pathetic flutter in his chest. He suppressed it beneath layers of ancient pride. "Good morning to you too, Lilith. You’re looking wonderfully vindictive today." She stopped at the edge of his desk, crossing her arms. "Don't try to charm me. I'm here in a strictly professional capacity." "Naturally," Lucifer said, leaning back. The Iron Throne groaned, tilting a perilous fifteen degrees to the left. Barnaby’s chewing intensified. *Grind. Gnaw. Squeal.* "And you came all the way up to the ninth circle just to tell me about a plumbing issue in the blood lakes?" Lilith’s eyes narrowed. "I take pride in my work. Unlike some people, who let their pets eat the furniture." She gestured sharply at Barnaby. The hound’s left head growled at her, while the right head continued chewing the iron. "He's teething," Lucifer defended weakly. "And I’ve been busy. Do you have any idea how much paperwork is involved when a televangelist actually makes it down here? The irony department has been working overtime." "You look tired," Lilith said. The barb was gone from her voice, replaced by an observational neutrality that was somehow worse. She reached out, idly reorganizing a stack of damnation warrants on his desk. It was a domestic, intimate gesture. It made Lucifer’s skin prickle. "I’m running a realm of eternal suffering, Lilith. It’s not exactly a spa retreat." He paused, watching her hands. "Though I suppose it’s been quieter without your... redecorating." During their last breakup, she had redecorated his penthouse by filling it with aggressive, carnivorous orchids. It had taken him a month to find his favorite cufflinks. "I missed the screams," she admitted softly, looking away toward the stained-glass window that depicted the Fall. "The abyss is peaceful, but it lacks ambiance. And the demons down there don't know how to make a decent macchiato." *Crunch. Scrape.* "Barnaby, I swear to My Father, I will turn you into a throw rug," Lucifer hissed, gripping the armrests as the throne dipped another inch. Lilith’s lip twitched. It was a microscopic movement, but Lucifer had spent millennia studying her face. She was fighting a smile. "You need to establish boundaries, Lucifer," she said, leaning against his desk. "With the dog, with the dukes of Hell. With everyone." "I am the literal Prince of Darkness," he pointed out. "I invented boundaries. I drew a line in the cosmic sand." "And then you let a puppy eat your chair." "He’s not a puppy, he’s an apex predator of the underworld!" As if on cue, Barnaby sneezed. A gout of hellfire shot from his nostrils, singeing the edges of a highly sensitive treaty with the Vatican. The dog looked up, gave a goofy, three-tongued pant, and went back to gnawing the iron. Lucifer buried his face in his hands. "I am so incredibly lonely," he muttered into his palms, entirely by accident. The silence that followed was heavier than the crushing gravity of the Envy ward. Lucifer froze, horrified by his own admission. He was the Morningstar. He did not do vulnerability. He did wrath. He did pride. He did not do sad-divorced-dad energy. He peeked through his fingers, expecting her to be holding a dagger, or at least a mocking sneer. Instead, Lilith was looking at him with a strange, dark softness. She walked around the desk, her heels clicking against the obsidian. She stopped beside the ruined throne, reached down, and firmly swatted Barnaby on the nose. "Leave it," she commanded. Barnaby whimpered, dropping the iron leg instantly. He slunk away to a corner, curling into a sulky, shadowy ball. Lilith turned her attention back to Lucifer. She didn't hug him—they were demons, not characters in a sitcom—but she did reach out and straighten his tie. Her fingers lingered against his collar. "The blood lakes really are a mess," she said quietly. "I'll have Beelzebub look into the sulfur vents," Lucifer replied, his voice equally hushed. "Don't send Beelzebub. He's an idiot. You should come down and inspect it yourself." She met his eyes, her gaze ancient and devastating. "Around eight? We could get dinner after. There's a new place in the Gluttony ring. I hear the suffering is farm-to-table." Lucifer felt the corners of his mouth tug upward. "I think I could pencil that in." "Good." Lilith stepped back, the fierce, unapproachable mask sliding flawlessly back into place. "And fix your chair, Luce. You look ridiculous." She turned and marched out of the throne room, the heavy doors slamming shut behind her with a satisfying, dramatic boom. Lucifer sat in the silence for a long moment. The screaming of the damned seemed a little more melodic now. He picked up his pen, pulled the damp-sock requisition form toward him, and smiled. From the corner, Barnaby let out a tentative whine. "Oh, come here, you idiot," Lucifer sighed. The hellhound bounded over, all three tails wagging, and rested his massive, sulfurous chins on Lucifer’s knee. The Iron Throne groaned, teetered on its three remaining legs, and finally collapsed backward, sending the Lord of Hell sprawling onto the floor in a tangle of limbs, paperwork, and hellhound. Lucifer lay on the cold obsidian, staring up at the vaulted ceiling. He laughed. It was a rusty, unused sound, but it felt remarkably like heaven.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece that fulfills the prompt's core requirements with genuine skill. The day-in-the-life structure is maintained, the on-again/off-again dynamic is clearly rendered through Lilith's "professional capacity" visit, and the dark comedy emerges naturally from the juxtaposition of cosmic horror with bureaucratic mundanity (Torment Processing Sheets, damp-sock requisitions, televangelist paperwork). The Gaiman influence shows in the wry, matter-of-fact treatment of the mythic. Strengths: The Barnaby hellhound thread is an excellent running gag that also functions as a physical barometer of Lucifer's domestic neglect. The dialogue is sharp and character-differentiated—Lilith's clipped professionalism masking affection, Lucifer's deflection through pride. The "not tried to assassinate him in weeks = 'u up' text" line is a standout. The tie-straightening gesture instead of a hug is well-judged restraint, explicitly acknowledged in-text ("they were demons, not characters in a sitcom"), which is both a strength and a slight self-congratulatory tic. Weaknesses: The piece leans on familiar beats. The "sad-divorced-dad energy" and "farm-to-table suffering" jokes are the kind of quippy register that risks feeling like a template (Pratchett/Gaiman pastiche rather than Gaiman himself). The accidental vulnerability confession ("I am so incredibly lonely") is convenient and slightly contrived—a more earned slip would have taken more setup. The ending's throne collapse into laughter is charming but tidier than the prompt's ambivalence might warrant; the reconciliation happens a touch easily, though the prompt does ask for the cycle "coming around," so it's defensible. Some metaphors strain ("dying breath of a suffocating star" is a bit much; "despair of orphaned Victorian children" is good). Minor purple moments exist but are controlled. The piece is coherent, well-paced, never meandering, and the prose flows cleanly. Overall: a polished, entertaining, professional piece that stops short of brilliance due to some predictability in its comic register and a slightly too-neat emotional resolution. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 76.8
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
The morning air in the *ludus* always smelled of the same three things: stale sweat, cold wood ash, and the metallic tang of old blood that never quite washed out of the porous stone floors. I woke before the sun, as I always did, my internal clock set to the harsh rhythms of captivity. Above me, the ceiling of my cramped cell was a canvas of shadows, painted by the flickering light of the corridor torches. I sat up, my joints popping in a familiar, agonizing chorus. My right shoulder, a souvenir from a Thracian’s curved blade three months prior, throbbed with a dull, rhythmic ache. I reached for the small clay jar beside my straw pallet, dipping two fingers into the fragrant mixture of olive oil and crushed rosemary. I massaged it into the thick, jagged scar tissue, the scent a sharp, clean contrast to the heavy musk of the sleeping quarters. Rising, I stepped to the small alcove carved into the stone wall of my cell. Inside sat a crude, wooden figurine of Hercules. He was my patron, the deity I whispered to when the nights grew too cold and the days too bloody. I didn't pray to Mars; the God of War cared only for the clash of armies and the fall of empires. But Hercules? He understood the burden of impossible labors. He understood what it meant to be a mortal bound by the whims of cruel masters, forced into the dirt and the muck to earn a divinity that was always just out of reach. I touched the worn wood of his lion-skin cloak, bowing my head. *Grant me the strength of the Nemean lion today,* I prayed silently. *Not for the crowd, but for myself.* The heavy iron gates at the end of the corridor groaned open, the sound echoing down the stone hallway like the bellow of a dying beast. It was time for the morning meal. I joined the silent procession of men filing out of their cells. We were a brotherhood forged in the fires of absolute subjugation, yet we rarely spoke. What was there to say? Today's friend was tomorrow's opponent. We shuffled into the mess hall, our bare feet slapping against the cold stones. Breakfast was *sagina*, a thick, tasteless porridge made of boiled barley and beans, designed to pack a layer of fat over our muscles to protect our vital organs from shallow cuts. I took my wooden bowl from the silent kitchen slave and sat at one of the long, splintering trestle tables. I ate mechanically, washing the paste down with watered-down vinegar that stung the back of my throat. Through the high, iron-grated windows of the mess hall, the sounds of Rome were beginning to bleed into our isolated world. The city was waking. I could hear the distant, rhythmic clatter of iron-rimmed cartwheels on the basalt paving stones of the Via Sacra, carrying goods to the markets. I could smell the faint, tantalizing aroma of baking bread from the *pistrina* down the street, mingling with the ever-present stench of the city’s open sewers and the smoke of a thousand hearth fires. As I chewed the bland barley, I listened to the murmurs of the older gladiators at the end of the table. They were whispering about the Emperor. Domitian was growing paranoid, they said, seeing assassins in every shadow of the Palatine Hill. To appease the restless plebeians—who were growing hungry due to the delayed grain shipments from Egypt—he had decreed a massive fifteen-day spectacle at the Flavian Amphitheatre. "Bread and circuses," I muttered into my cup, the bitter vinegar burning my lips. It was the oldest trick in the Republic, carried seamlessly into the Empire. Keep the bellies full enough to prevent a riot, and keep the eyes dazzled by slaughter so they don't look too closely at the men in purple hoarding the wealth of the known world. We were the circuses. Our blood, spilled on the imported white sand of the arena, was the mortar that held the crumbling social order together. Out there, beyond the walls of the *ludus*, patricians reclined on silk cushions, gorging on flamingo tongues and dormice rolled in honey, while the common folk fought over scraps in the Subura. And we, the lowest of the low, the condemned, the enslaved, were elevated to the status of demigods for a fleeting afternoon, solely to distract the masses from their own miserable chains. Our *lanista*, a rotund man named Valerius whose wealth was built entirely on our suffering, entered the hall. He wore a pristine white tunic bordered in purple, a stark contrast to our rough, unbleached wool loincloths. He surveyed us not as men, but as an investor surveys his livestock. His eyes lingered on me for a moment, calculating the sesterces I could bring him in the upcoming games. I met his gaze with a blank, unreadable stare. To show emotion was to show weakness. The meal ended with the sharp crack of a guard’s staff against the wooden table. We rose in unison, filing out toward the training courtyard. The sun was fully up now, cresting the high walls of the *ludus* and baking the packed earth of the yard. The heat was already oppressive, wrapping around us like a damp wool blanket. I walked to the weapon racks, my hand bypassing the cold, heavy steel of the *gladius*. Today was for the *rudis*, the heavy wooden training swords. I gripped the smooth, worn handle of the wooden blade. It was heavier than real steel, designed to build our endurance, but it represented something far more profound. The *rudis* was the symbol of freedom. If a gladiator survived long enough, fought brilliantly enough, the Emperor might present him with a wooden sword, severing his bonds to the arena forever. I swung the wooden sword in a slow, deliberate arc, the air whistling over the dull edge. Every muscle in my back and arms pulled tight, a symphony of disciplined power. I closed my eyes, letting the heat of the Roman sun beat down on my face, smelling the dust kicked up by a hundred pacing men. I thought of Hercules again, of his final labor, dragging the three-headed hound from the depths of the underworld into the light of the sun. The arena was my underworld, and the roaring crowd was the beast I had to tame. I opened my eyes, staring at the high, impenetrable stone walls that separated me from the sprawling, chaotic heart of the Empire. I was a prisoner, a pawn in a political game much larger than myself, a piece of meat meant to pacify a starving city. But with the wooden sword in my hand, feeling the solid, undeniable reality of my own strength, I knew I was still alive. And as long as I breathed, the final labor was not yet finished.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent, polished slice-of-life that fulfills nearly every instruction: first person, past tense, roughly 1000 words, no combat, rich sensory detail (ash, blood-stained stone, barley porridge, vinegar, baking bread, sewers), interiority through the narrator's prayers and reflections, and a clear political frame (Domitian's paranoia, grain shortages, "bread and circuses" as social pacification). The Hercules devotion is a nice characterizing touch, and the *rudis* as a symbol of freedom gives the ending thematic weight without resorting to sentimentality. Weaknesses: the material is well-trodden. The cynical-but-noble gladiator, the greedy *lanista*, the "we were the circuses" political commentary—all of it is familiar to the point of predictability. Some images are stock ("brotherhood forged in the fires of absolute subjugation," "damp wool blanket" of heat). The political exposition, delivered via whispering older gladiators, is efficient but slightly convenient—a touch of tell-don't-show in service of the prompt's requirements. The prose is clean and controlled but rarely surprising; it reads like skilled genre work rather than distinctive literature. There is essentially no dialogue beyond a muttered line, so dialogue quality is hard to assess and largely excluded. The ending lands its "still alive / labor unfinished" note believably, earned by the established Hercules motif, so no incongruent positivity or unearned transformation. Voice is consistent throughout, appropriately weary and restrained. Emotionally it engages but at a simmer; the narrator's guardedness, while in character, keeps the reader at a slight distance. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 82.2
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**4 March 1974** Dear Ma, I made it out in one piece. The boat ride from Stromness was rough enough to rattle my back teeth loose, but we got ashore before the tide turned against us. The lighthouse is a beast of a thing when you’re standing right under it. Sule Skerry is just a slab of rock, really. Barely a blade of grass to be seen, just guano and puddles. The principal keeper, a gruff old boy named MacBride, showed me my bunk and put me straight to work polishing the brasses. He’s not one for small talk, which I suppose suits the job. From the gallery, you can see Stack Skerry jutting out of the water to the west like a rotten black tooth. The sea smashes right against it. It’s a fair view, I’ll give it that. The quiet takes some getting used to. Back in Peterhead, there’s always the sound of the trawlers or the gulls or the bairns in the street. Here, it’s just the wind and the generator hum. Don't worry about me. The wage is good, and I’ll send the bulk of it back with the relief boat next month. Buy yourself some decent coal for a change. Love, Callum *** **18 March 1974** My Dear Son, Thank the Lord you’re safe. I couldn’t sleep a wink the night you left, listening to the wind howling round the chimney and thinking of you out on that awful rock. I don’t need your money, Callum. I’ve managed on my own since your Da passed, and I’ll manage now. You save it for yourself. You’re twenty-two, you should be putting it aside for a house, or a lassie, not keeping your old mother in coal. But I appreciate the thought, I do. Auntie Jean came round yesterday with half a dozen eggs and her usual gossip. She says the shipyard is taking on fitters again. I know you said you were sick of the noise and the dirt, but it’s steady work, and it’s on dry land. Just think about it. I’ve sent a tin of shortbread with the Northern Lighthouse Board supply boat. Share it with Mr. MacBride. Make sure you’re eating proper hot meals. All my love, Ma *** **12 May 1974** Dear Ma, Thanks for the shortbread. MacBride ate half the tin in one sitting without so much as a thank you, but I suppose that’s just his way. The weather turned foul on Tuesday and hasn't let up. The fog is so thick you can’t see the bottom of the tower from the lantern room. We’ve had the foghorn sounding every ninety seconds for four days. It shakes the dust out of the ceiling and vibrates right in your breastbone. You can’t sleep through it. You just lie in your bunk, waiting for the next blast. I’ll admit, Ma, the isolation is starting to bite. I haven’t heard a new voice in two months. MacBride only speaks to bark orders about the logbook or the paraffin levels. Yesterday, I caught myself talking out loud to a dead storm petrel I found on the gallery grating. I keep looking out toward Stack Skerry when the fog thins, just to prove to myself there’s something else in the world besides this tower. I miss the pub. I miss the smell of chips from the shop on the corner. I even miss the noise of the shipyard. Don't fret, though. I've signed the contract for the year. I’m no quitter. Love, Callum *** **28 May 1974** Callum, Your letter broke my heart. I can hear the exhaustion in your words. There is no shame in coming home, son. Being a quitter is leaving a job undone, but preserving your own mind is just common sense. Your Da used to get that same trapped look in his eyes when he was out on the deep-water trawlers for too long. He’d come back to us and he’d sit in the armchair, staring right through the television, his hands shaking. The sea takes a toll on men, Callum. It empties them out. I won't let it do that to you. I spoke to Mr. Henderson at the yard. He said there’s a place for you in the fabrication shed whenever you want it. Please, son. Speak to the superintendent when the relief boat comes. Love, Ma *** **14 September 1974** Dear Ma, I’m sorry I haven’t written the last two boats. I haven't had the energy to hold a pen. The autumn gales started early. For three weeks, the waves have been breaking completely over the rock. We can’t even step outside the heavy oak doors at the base of the tower. The water just obliterates everything. I feel like a ghost, Ma. I wind the clockwork mechanism. I trim the wicks. I polish the lenses. But I don't feel like I'm really here. Last night, I was standing up in the lantern room staring out at the pitch black. I couldn't see Stack Skerry. I couldn't see the sea. I couldn't even see my own reflection in the glass. I felt like if I just opened the storm door and stepped out, the wind would scatter me like ash. MacBride caught me with my hand on the latch. He didn't yell. He just pulled me back, locked it, and put the kettle on. He told me the rock breaks everyone eventually. You were right about Da. I finally understand why he drank when he got ashore. He was trying to fill the silence the sea left inside him. I don't want that silence, Ma. Tell Henderson I’ll take the job. Love, Callum *** **2 October 1974** Callum! Oh, thank God. Thank God. I am weeping at the kitchen table as I write this. I have already been round to the yard. Henderson expects you on the first of November. I’ve aired out your old room and washed all the bedding. Auntie Jean is bringing over a terrible looking meat pie to celebrate, but I’ve bought a lovely bit of beef for a proper Sunday roast the day you get back. Just hold on, son. The boat will be there in three weeks. Keep your head down, do your work, and pack your bags. We are going to get you warm, and we are going to get you fed, and you never have to look at that awful grey water again. I am so proud of you for knowing when to walk away. All my love, Ma *** **24 October 1974** Dear Ma, I’m writing this from my bunk, with my duffel bag packed and sitting at the foot of the bed. The relief boat is due in three hours. The sky is clear, and the sea is flat and blue. It almost looks peaceful, but I know better now. I went out onto the gallery one last time this morning. I looked over at Stack Skerry, standing there taking the battering of the waves, day in and day out. It’s strong, but it’s slowly wearing away. That would have been me if I stayed. I feel a weight lifting off my chest that I didn’t even fully realize was there. I’m looking forward to the noise of the yard. I’m looking forward to the dirt on my hands that isn't brass polish or paraffin. But mostly, I’m just looking forward to sitting at the kitchen table and hearing you and Auntie Jean blethering on about the neighbors. Put the kettle on, Ma. I’m coming home. Love, Callum
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This epistolary story is a strong execution of the brief. The letters span roughly eight months, chart Callum's psychological decline on Sule Skerry and his decision to leave. The Scottish working-class voices are well differentiated: Callum's letters are plain, wry, and concrete; his mother's are warmer, fussier, and gently pushy. Both feel period-appropriate (1974, Northern Lighthouse Board, paraffin lamps, relief boats) and the details—guano, foghorn every ninety seconds, brass polishing, storm petrel—do real work establishing isolation without stating it outright. The plot unfolds gradually and believably: initial bravado, then creeping loneliness, then a genuine crisis (the hand on the storm door latch), then resolution. The mother's counter-correspondence—refusing money, invoking the dead father's trawler trauma, arranging the shipyard job—gives her agency and a distinct motivation. The father parallel is the emotional spine, and it lands because it's revealed through the mother first and confirmed by Callum later. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 72.8
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The hostess stand at *Bistro 42* is running a point-of-sale system on an exposed subnet. I know this because the terminal is facing the window, and I can literally see the default Windows 7 taskbar hiding beneath the restaurant software. A script kiddie with a spoofed MAC address and five minutes on the guest Wi-Fi could dump the day’s credit card receipts. *Stop it,* I tell myself. *Eyes forward. Port scan disabled.* I take a sip of my water, forcing my gaze back to the woman sitting across from me. Clara. She has kind eyes, a nervous but genuine smile, and absolutely terrible situational awareness. She left her purse hanging on the back of her chair, a textbook vector for a brush-pass theft. *Focus. Human connection. Act like a person, not a packet sniffer.* "So," Clara says, swirling her Pinot Noir, "I was a little nervous about tonight. The apps are such a gamble." "Total roll of the dice," I agree, offering a practiced, non-threatening smile. Internally, I’m analyzing the metadata of her dating profile that brought us here. She’d uploaded photos with full EXIF data intact; I knew her favorite coffee shop and the exact GPS coordinates of her office before we even said hello. I didn’t look for it maliciously. It’s just the curse. When you spend a decade finding the cracks in the world's digital foundations—first for the thrill, now for a corporate paycheck—you can't turn off the blacklight. You see the stains everywhere. But tonight is actually going well. Anomalously well. The firewall between us had dropped significantly about twenty minutes ago when I made a casual joke about "resource management," and she countered with a reference to mana-screw. It turned out Clara is a *Magic: The Gathering* player. Not just a casual, either. She runs a blue-black Dimir control deck. It makes perfect sense; she’s calculating, likes to keep her options open, and prefers to counter threats before they hit the board. As a former black-hat, I respect the hell out of a good control player. We both understand the mechanics of exploiting an opponent's missteps. "It’s just wild," Clara continues, leaning in, the candlelight catching her features. "I haven't met anyone else who plays paper Magic in years. Usually, it's just me and my brother. We learned together back when we lived on Elm Street." *Security Question 1: What was the name of the street you grew up on? Elm.* I nod, smiling. "Nothing beats the physical cards. The tactile feel." "Exactly! Though my mom hated it. She thought it was demonic or something. Classic Mrs. Abernathy, right?" She laughs. "Well, she goes by Abernathy now, but she was a Higgins back then. Fierce Irish Catholic." *Security Question 2: What is your mother’s maiden name? Higgins.* My brain logs the data automatically into a mental text file. I don't want to know this. I want to look at the way her hair falls across her shoulder. I want to enjoy the shared rhythm of a good date. But her conversational opsec is a nightmare. She is practically handing me the keys to her digital kingdom in the form of charming, self-deprecating anecdotes. "I had to hide my cards under my mattress," she says. "Right next to my first dog’s bed. Poor Buster. He was a terrible guard dog, but a great secret keeper." *Security Question 3: What was the name of your first pet? Buster.* *Elm. Higgins. Buster.* I could reset her banking password right now. I could hijack her email, pivot to her social media, and own her entire digital identity before the entrees arrive. *Shut up, brain. Enjoy the date.* "I ran a red deck back then," I say, forcing my mind back to the analog world. "Aggro. Burn everything down as fast as possible." "Ah," Clara smirks. "A goblin player. I should have known. You seem like the type who likes to move fast and break things." My heart does a strange, unfamiliar flutter. A successful ping. She gets it. She gets *me*. This is the closest I’ve felt to another human being in months. The evening is perfectly balanced. Then, her phone buzzes on the table. It’s an Android device. Unencrypted lock screen notifications. I can see it's a text from someone named 'Sarah'. Clara sighs, picking up the device. "Sorry, let me just silence this. My roommate locked herself out again." She wakes the screen. And right there, in front of God, me, and the unpatched POS system at the hostess stand, Clara places her thumb on the screen and draws an 'L' shape on the 3x3 pattern grid. Top left, down to bottom left, across to bottom right. My breath catches. It’s the visual equivalent of a screeching modem. It is, statistically, the second most common, easily guessable unlock pattern in the world, right behind the 'Z'. Furthermore, I can clearly see the greasy smudge trail permanently etched into her screen protector, broadcasting the password to anyone within a ten-foot radius. Before the rational, reformed, socially-adjusted part of my brain can engage the emergency brakes, my mouth opens. "You know a toddler with a brute-force script could bypass that, right?" The words hang in the air, suspended over the table like a bad smell. Clara stops, her thumb hovering over the glass. She looks up, the warmth instantly draining from her eyes. The Dimir player has recognized a threat. Shields are up. Counterspell cast. "Excuse me?" she says, her voice dropping an octave. *Critical error. Social protocol violation. Attempting rollback.* "I just... your pattern," I stammer, my internal cooling fans spinning up as I start to sweat. "It's an 'L'. And there's a smudge. Anyone who steals your phone wouldn't even have to guess. They'd just follow the grease." Silence. The ambient noise of the restaurant seems to vanish. Clara slowly places the phone face down on the table. "You were watching me unlock my phone?" she asks, the word 'creep' heavily implied in her tone. "No! I mean, yes, but not intentionally," I backpedal, desperately trying to patch the vulnerability I just blew wide open. "It's an occupational hazard. I work in cybersecurity. Penetration testing. I literally get paid to look for weaknesses in systems. It’s hard to turn off." She crosses her arms. The physical manifestation of a closed port. "So you sit on dates and look for weaknesses in the women you're out with?" *Ouch. Direct hit to the root directory.* "No," I say softly, dropping the defensive posture. "I look for weaknesses in everything. The restaurant's Wi-Fi. The waiter's habit of leaving the receipt book open. It's a paranoia I can't shake. But with you..." I take a breath. Honesty is the only exploit left that might work. "With you, I was actually having a hard time focusing on the flaws. Because I was too busy enjoying the connection. Until the 'L' pattern. That was just... a bridge too far for my neurotic brain. I'm sorry." Clara stares at me for a long, agonizing moment. I can see her processing the data, running it through her own internal heuristic analysis. Is he a threat? Is he just weird? Slowly, the corner of her mouth twitches upward. "An 'L' is that bad, huh?" she asks. "It’s catastrophic," I admit, releasing a breath I didn't realize I was holding. She picks up the phone, navigates to the security settings, and slides it across the table to me. "Alright, Mr. Cybersecurity. Set a new one. Something a goblin player couldn't break." I look at the blank grid, then up at her. The connection is still active. The session hasn't timed out. I smile, reach out, and draw a complex, sprawling, intersecting polygon. "Memorize this," I tell her. "And for the love of God, wipe your screen on your shirt once in a while."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece executes the prompt with strong fidelity: first-person internal monologue dominates, the white-hat hacker's compulsive vulnerability-scanning is established immediately (the POS system, the purse, the EXIF data), the MTG connection is developed naturally through deck-choice characterization (Dimir control vs. red aggro is a genuinely clever mirror of their personalities), and the unlock-pattern faux pas lands on cue with a satisfying payoff where Clara hands him the phone to set a new pattern. Strengths: The security-question gag (Elm, Higgins, Buster) is a well-structured escalation that shows rather than tells the protagonist's involuntary data harvesting. The tech metaphors ("closed port," "counterspell cast," "session hasn't timed out") are consistent with the character's worldview and mostly earn their place. The MTG framing doubles as characterization for both parties. Dialogue is serviceable and Clara gets a believable arc from warmth to offense to cautious re-engagement. Weaknesses: The metaphor layer is relentless to the point of predictability—nearly every paragraph contains a firewall, ping, or rollback reference, and some are strained ("direct hit to the root directory," "visual equivalent of a screeching modem"). The prose is competent but workmanlike; the restaurant, Clara, and the atmosphere are sketched thinly (candlelight catching her features is stock). Clara's forgiveness arrives a bit quickly and conveniently—the "long, agonizing moment" is asserted rather than dramatized, and her pivot to playful trust is lightly earned. The ending is tidy and charming but borders on sitcom neatness. The "second most common pattern, right behind the Z" factoid is a nice touch of authenticity, though the smudge-trail observation is a well-worn trope in security writing. Emotionally, the piece is engaging but not deep; the loneliness is stated ("closest I've felt to another human being in months") rather than fully excavated. Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
*Squeak.* The projector wheel turns, advancing to a slide on cellular respiration, and Mr. Harrison’s voice drones on, but I am entirely consumed by the gravitational pull of the boy sitting exactly eighteen inches to my left. Eighteen inches. I know this because I discretely measured the distance using the standard length of my No. 2 pencil (seven point five inches) as a visual reference while pretending to retrieve a dropped eraser. Leo. *Squeak.* We are supposed to be designing a terrarium. A closed ecosystem. Which is ironic, considering I am currently trapped in the suffocating, hermetically sealed ecosystem of my own mind. Okay, Maya, focus. You need to say something. You are partners. Partners speak to each other. They exchange ideas. They do not sit in paralyzed, mute agony staring at the laminate grain of the science table. I need an opening line. Something casual, yet indicating a firm grasp of the biological principles at play, but absolutely not sounding like I swallowed the textbook. *Drafting Option A:* "So, Leo, thinking about going moss-heavy for the autotrophs?" *Critique:* Too eager. The word "heavy" implies a level of enthusiasm for bryophytes that borders on the psychopathic. Plus, what if he hates moss? What if he thinks moss is boring? Then I’m the weird moss girl for the rest of eighth grade. Scratch Option A. *Squeak.* Mr. Harrison points a red laser at a diagram of a stomata. Leo shifts in his stool. His knee—clad in faded denim—moves roughly two inches closer to mine. My sympathetic nervous system immediately interprets this as a mortal threat, dumping a gallon of adrenaline into my bloodstream. My heart rate accelerates to a frantic, fluttering rhythm, a trapped bird battering against my ribs. I need to control my breathing. Inhale for four seconds. Hold for four. Exhale for four. If I breathe too loudly, he’ll hear my respiratory distress. I try to arrange my face into an expression of placid academic interest. Not a frown, which reads as hostile, but not a smile, which reads as deranged. A neutral, pleasant baseline. I must look like a mannequin. A sweating, hyperventilating mannequin. *Drafting Option B:* "I was reviewing the rubric, and it seems optimizing the carbon-oxygen cycle is our primary objective." *Critique:* Insufferable. I sound like a corporate middle manager trying to synergize a quarterly report. He’ll think I’m an arrogant know-it-all who plans to micromanage the dirt and the ferns. I am articulate in my head—I have a vocabulary in the ninety-ninth percentile, according to standardized testing—but the moment I attempt to translate these complex thoughts into vocalized sound, my vocal cords stage a mutiny. The syllables curdle on my tongue. *Squeak.* "Notice the condensation," Mr. Harrison says. I am noticing the condensation. It is currently forming on my palms. I wipe them surreptitiously on my jeans, timing the movement with Mr. Harrison’s pacing so it looks like a natural readjustment of my posture. What do normal people do with their hands? Right now, my hands feel like heavy, useless appendages. If I cross my arms, I’m defensive. If I leave them on the table, I look like I’m waiting for a manicure. I settle for lightly gripping the edge of my notebook, knuckles white. *Squeak.* Leo sighs. It’s a quiet, breathy sound. Is he bored? Is he annoyed he got paired with me? He probably wanted to be partnered with Chloe. Chloe doesn't have to rehearse her sentences. Chloe just opens her mouth and words tumble out, fully formed, sparkling with effortless charisma. If Chloe were sitting here, she’d probably bump his shoulder and say something mildly teasing about his handwriting, and he would laugh. I can't bump his shoulder. If I bumped his shoulder, I would probably miscalculate the force and knock him off his stool, resulting in a concussion and a trip to the nurse, forever cementing my legacy as the girl who physically assaulted him during a botany assignment. *Drafting Option C:* "Do you have any preference for the substrate layer?" *Critique:* Substrate? Really, Maya? Who says substrate casually? Just say dirt. No, soil. Soil is scientific. Dirt is what you track into the house. "Do you want to pick the soil?" Too blunt. Too demanding. Why is this so difficult? It’s just English. Nouns, verbs, syntax. I understand the mechanics of language perfectly. Yet, the bridge between my brain and my mouth has been entirely washed out by a flood of cortisol. I am acutely aware of every microscopic movement I make. If I blink too much, I’ll look manic. If I don’t blink enough, I’ll look like a serial killer. *Squeak.* "Alright, you have the rest of the period to brainstorm with your partner," Mr. Harrison announces. The projector hums, finally still. The fluorescent lights flicker on. The moment of truth. The deadline is here. The ecosystem is open. Leo turns his head. His eyes are hazel. I hadn't noticed that before. They have little flecks of gold in them, like mineral deposits in metamorphic rock. Stop thinking about rocks. He leans forward, resting his elbows on the black laminate top. He spins his pencil through his fingers. He’s going to speak first. Oh god, he’s going to speak first, and I won’t have a script prepared for whatever he says. My mind races, trying to predict the infinite branching paths of his potential dialogue. "So," Leo says. His voice is a little gravelly, still finding its permanent pitch. "So," I reply in my head. *A brilliant retort, Maya. Truly, you are the conversationalist of our generation.* He stops spinning the pencil. "I'm really bad at keeping plants alive. Like, I killed a cactus once. So... you might have to take the lead on the actual living stuff." He killed a cactus. The humor in this statement registers in my prefrontal cortex, but my facial muscles are still locked in their mannequin paralysis. Smile. You need to smile. A small, reassuring smile. I command my zygomaticus major muscles to contract. *Drafting Option D:* "Cacti are actually susceptible to root rot from overwatering, so it's a common misconception that they are foolproof. But don't worry, I have extensive experience with terrarium maintenance." *Critique:* Too long. Too pedantic. Condescending. *Drafting Option E:* "That's funny." *Critique:* Boring. Robotic. He is looking at me. Waiting. The silence is stretching, becoming a physical weight in the space between us. Three seconds. Four seconds. It’s too long. I’ve ruined it. He thinks I’m a mute freak. The anxiety peaks, a crescendo of static in my ears, drowning out the ambient chatter of the classroom. Just speak. Just say literally anything. I open my mouth. The polished, articulate, ninety-ninth-percentile vocabulary evaporates, leaving behind only the raw, panicked instinct of survival. "I won't let you kill our moss," I say. My voice sounds thin, a little too quiet, but it doesn't crack. Leo looks at me for a split second, and my stomach plummets. I said moss. I went with Option A. I am the weird moss girl. Then, the corner of his mouth twitches upward. He lets out a short, genuine laugh. "Awesome," he says. "Because I was definitely going to suggest we go moss-heavy." My heart stutters, then settles into a new, slightly less frantic rhythm. I exhale, a tiny, silent breath, and loosen my white-knuckled grip on the notebook. The projector is off, but in my head, the loudest squeak of the day just finally fell silent.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong execution of the prompt: an 8th-grade girl's internal monologue during a science class, cycling through drafted conversational options with self-critiques, hyper-awareness of body language, and the gap between her articulate inner voice and stunted speech. The "Drafting Option / Critique" structure is a clever formal device that dramatizes overthinking rather than merely describing it. The recurring *Squeak* of the projector wheel provides rhythm and time-marking. The ending—she blurts "I won't let you kill our moss" and Leo laughs, having independently planned moss—lands as a small, believable payoff rather than a fantasy transformation; the anxiety isn't cured, just slightly loosened, which is appropriately modest. Strengths: consistent ironic, precise voice; good physical detail (pencil-measured eighteen inches, white knuckles, timing a hand-wipe to the teacher's pacing); the humor feels age-appropriate and character-driven; the science-class setting is used thematically (closed ecosystem, stomata, condensation as metaphors for her own state) without becoming gimmicky. Weaknesses: the voice occasionally reads older than 8th grade—"synergize a quarterly report," "conversationalist of our generation," "mineral deposits in metamorphic rock"—though this is partly justified by the premise of an articulate inner narrator, and the prompt explicitly asks for that gap. Some metaphors are stacked a bit densely (trapped bird, curdling syllables, cortisol flood), tipping toward overwrought in places. The Chloe comparison and the "knock him off his stool" bit are familiar anxiety-monologue tropes; the piece doesn't break much new ground in the genre of anxious-crush interiority. The ending's neatness (he was going to suggest moss too) is a touch convenient, but it's small enough to feel earned as lightness rather than saccharine. Dialogue is minimal but the little there is (Leo's cactus line) is natural and believable.
